THE SMALLEST FISH IN THE WORLD

Before 1925, the "tabios" was thought to have been the smallest fish in the
world. A full-grown "tabios" measured a fraction over eleven millimeters. The
"tabios" is found in Lake Buhi, in the Bicol Region of Luzon.

In 1925, Dr. Albert Herre, an ichthyologist, was assigned by the American
government to identify and describe Philippine fishes. From a collection of the
Philippine National Museum, he found the prototypes of a still smaller type of fish.
There were 75 of the tiny fish which he named Pandaka Pygmaea in a bottle. They
were so small that the "tabios" appeared big by comparison.

When Dr. Herre went back to the
United States, he sent a few specimens
to   the     Stanford    National    Science
Museum.       Dr.   Herre’s   findings   were
doubted because this fish remained a
rarity. No one had ever seen a live
specimen of the fish that Dr. Herre
claimed was the smallest fish in the
world.

On February 28, 1951, Ricardo Esguerra, one of the marine biologists
working in the saltwater experiments station of the Bureau of Fisheries in Malabon,
Rizal, excitedly called up the Bureau’s main office and announced that he had
found live specimens of the Pandaka. Inocencio Ronquillo, an expert of the
Bureau, hurried to the experiment station and studied the tiny fish which had
eluded scientists for many years. He measured and weighed them. To confirm his
findings, Ronquillo wrote to the curator of Stanford University Museum of Natural
Science and asked for some specimens of the fish that Dr. Herre had taken before.

Finally, Dr. Leonard Schulz, the museum’s representative, pronounced that they
were one and the same type. Thus after 25 years, the Philippines could at least
claim to have the world’s smallest fish. The Pandaka has now been found in
various parts of the Philippines.

The smallest fish is known under the scientific name of Pandaka Pygmaea.
Samples have been sent to the museums and aquariums of cities all over the
world.

The Pandaka’s average length when full-grown is 9.66 millimeters or about the size
of a grain of rice. It has a moderately elongated body that is wedge-shaped
when viewed from above. Its head is large in proportion to its size. Its eyes protrude.
It has two rows of teeth on either side of the jaw, the outer teeth being larger and
more widely set than the inner row.

COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS

items.text: Why was the discovery of Pandaka pygmaea in the Philippines in 1925 considered historically important?
opts: It showed that all tabios populations had gone extinct
It was then regarded as the smallest known fish in the world
It was the first marine fish ever described from the Philippines
It proved that all small fish in the Philippines were juveniles

items.text: What was Dr. Albert Herre’s main role in the history of Pandaka pygmaea?
opts: He first described and named Pandaka pygmaea in 1925
He reclassified tabios as Pandaka pygmaea in 1951
He proved that Pandaka pygmaea lives only in deep ocean trenches
He led a campaign to ban fishing of all small fish in the Philippines

items.text: How did Ricardo Esguerra contribute to the story of Pandaka pygmaea in 1951?
opts: He replaced Pandaka pygmaea with tabios in scientific classification
He officially declared Pandaka pygmaea extinct in the wild
He moved all remaining Pandaka pygmaea to foreign aquariums
He rediscovered Pandaka pygmaea in the Philippines after fears it had disappeared

items.text: In historical discussions, why is the local fish known as tabios often mentioned alongside Pandaka pygmaea?
opts: Tabios and Pandaka pygmaea are the same species under different general
Tabios is the scientific name that replaced Pandaka pygmaea
Tabios was initially thought to be the true smallest fish, later replaced by Pandaka pygmaea
Tabios is a local small fish whose fame was overshadowed by Pandaka pygmaea as the "smallest fish"

items.text: Which statement best describes the typical habitat historically associated with Pandaka pygmaea in the Philippines?
opts: Shallow coastal or estuarine areas, often near mangroves
High- altitude crater lakes far from the sea

items.text: From a biological perspective, why is the tiny adult size of Pandaka pygmaea scientifically intriguing?
opts: It demonstrates that only deep- sea fish can become very small
It challenges ideas about the lower size limits of vertebrate bodies
It proves that all small fish grow into large fish later
It shows that small fish cannot reproduce successfully

items.text: Historically, how did the "smallest fish in the world" label affect public and scientific attention toward Pandaka pygmaea?
opts: It shifted all attention away from Philippine biodiversity
It led to the immediate banning of all fishing in its habitat
It turned Pandaka pygmaea into a globally cited example of extreme miniaturization
It caused scientists to ignore Pandaka pygmaea as unimportant

items.text: What does the historical replacement of tabios in popular discussion by Pandaka pygmaea as the "smallest fish" mainly illustrate?
opts: That local fish names are always incorrect
That only foreign scientists can discover important species
That large fish are more important than small fish
That scientific records and media can reshape which species the public notices

items.text: Why is it important for modern students in the Philippines to learn about the historical discovery and rediscovery of Pandaka pygmaea?
opts: It teaches only that foreign scientists are superior
It shows that biodiversity is only found in other countries
It highlights the value of both foreign and Filipino contributions to understanding local biodiversity
It proves that small fishes are useless for food

items.text: What conservation lesson can be drawn from the story of Pandaka pygmaea’s small size and specialized habitat?
opts: Conservation is only needed in remote, untouched wilderness areas
Only large, commercially valuable fish deserve protection
Protecting mangroves and coastal wetlands can help safeguard even the smallest, most specialized species
Small fish are too numerous to be affected by habitat loss

LET THERE BE NO GRUDGES

This story is about a young boy who got into a fight with his elder
brother. Enoch is his name, and his elder brother would always pick on him
to the extent of making him angry and feeling bitter later.

One morning they were it again. They fought hard and exchanged
blows with each other. Somewhat outmatched because Enoch was
wanting in size and height, he took quite a beating. His elder brother’s
muscles were too much for him. His pride and ego suffered the most. The
whole incident left him bitter towards his elder brother. As a matter of fact,
he refused to talk or look at his brother. He was gritting his teeth with anger
for not being able to put up square fight.

Bedtime came. Their mother wanted
to pacify them and told them to make
up as soon as possible.

Enoch was still grumbling, but his eyes were fixed towards the elder
brother’s direction. Then the mother spoke to the younger one. “Don’t you
think you should forgive your brother before you go to bed?” Remember
the Bible says, “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath.”

The younger son looked toward his mother with perplexity. He
thought for a few seconds and then said, “Mother, how can I keep the sun
from going down?” The boy’s question revealed that he had no intention
of getting rid of his grudge.

So, the mother explained to her younger son and made him
understand what life would be like when people hold grudges against

each other. It is true that there are people with an unforgiving attitude and
true too, that we cannot change another person’s heart.

She further explained that we cannot keep the sun from going down.
But we can keep it from setting on your anger. And that means we must
forgive.

opts: "Don't let the sun go down on your wrath" b)"Love your neighbor"

THE VALUE OF WORK

Everything has value, no matter how insignificant or simple it is. At the
mere mention of work, one immediately connects with the idea of toil and
fatigue, which pertains to a slave who overdoes things in a difficult manner.
Everything in this world involves work.

In what light should work be viewed? Anything that comes from
something done is achieved by means of labor and work. It is of two-fold
nature, either mental or physical. Both are indispensable to the well-being
of human society. Our attention is directed towards physical labor.

Christianity teaches us to regard work as something sacred and
honorable. Work is duty. You must not only work hard, but you must also
love it wholeheartedly. Without it, order and cleanliness can never exist in
the house. A state of affairs would be a mess and discomfort would prevail.

People who work and stay
busy have no time for hanging
around, gossiping, or being with bad
company. Women who are fond of
work are more virtuous and purer.
There is no dull moment in their lives,
there is so much to gain when they
are physically occupied.

Be proud, therefore, and love your work. Do it diligently and make it your
best. Treat it as an inseparable friend. Whatever the nature of your work may be,

do it with care and diligence. If it is a domestic chore, do not find fault and
make critical remarks, but put your hand at everything.

If your work is to be really done well, if it is to gain merit for yourself,
perform it with a good intention. Yes, be patient, for without patience, no labor,
toil, or work can be meritorious in the eyes of someone above.

These lines speak well of this: Swiftly time speeds on its way. See that thou
use it well. Let each hour of every day be a tale of wisdom to tell.

What does Christianity teach about work?
What do people who work and stay busy avoid, per the passage?
opts: Hanging around, gossiping, or bad company

TAJ MAHAL: AN IMMORTAL MONUMENT TO AN EMPEROR’S LOVE

In Agra, India, stands an immortal monument to an emperor’s love. It
was built by Emperor Shah Jahan for his third wife, the beautiful Mumtaz
Mahal. Mumtaz, the queen, was born in 1593.

He was a good emperor, and he ruled wisely. During his reign,
magnificent buildings and palaces were built. He had a goldsmith build an
elaborate throne of rare gems. It was a long, low couch with golden legs. A
canopy, which rested on twelve emerald pillars, was over the throne. A
tree of diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and pearls stood beside it.

Then, in 1631, Queen Mumtaz Mahal died in childbirth. The emperor
was grief-stricken. He forbade music in his court, gave up wearing the
colored imperial robes, and wore only white for mourning. A sepulcher was
built for her. Twenty thousand workers labored 20 years to complete it. The
best artisans, sculptors, designers, and carvers in India and nearby countries
were employed under the most renowned architect of those days, Ustad
Ahmad.

The monument was made of precious stones and valuable materials.
The glorious white marble used comes from India; garnets and lapis lazuli come from
Ceylon. All in all, more than 40 varieties of precious stones were used, including
turquoise mined in Tibet.

On the north side of the great highway leading to the sepulcher, a tall
gateway, 80 feet high, guarded the entrance. The gateway doors were
made of silver and studded with semi-precious stones. No less beautiful are
the surroundings of the sepulcher. In the waters of the famous reflecting

pool, the image of the tall dome floats eternally in blue. Everything around
the place is made to draw the eyes to the central figure of the immortal
monument to an emperor’s love, the Taj Mahal.

COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS

opts: He prioritized military conquests over arts
He valued opulence and skilled craftsmanship

items.text: Why might the emperor's choice of white robes after Mumtaz's death symbolize more than simple mourning?
opts: It honored the workers' marble labor
It matched the silver gateway colors
It showed his preference for plain fashion
It represented purity of his undying devotion

items.text: What does the involvement of artisans from "India and nearby countries" suggest about the monument's purpose?
opts: To make it a universal symbol of grief and love
To limit it to local Indian traditions
To create the cheapest possible structure

items.text: How does the reflecting pool's design infer the Taj Mahal's intended emotional impact?
opts: It hides flaws in the marble construction
It evokes eternal beauty mirroring the love
It creates a sense of fleeting impermanence
It focuses attention on the highway gateway

items.text: What broader inference can be drawn about Mumtaz Mahal's role in Shah Jahan's life from the monument's scale?
opts: She influenced only his architectural tastes
Her death had little effect on his reign
She was a minor consort among many
She was central to his personal and ruling identity ​

NO LOVE, NO VICTORY

Love is an indispensable necessity for every human heart. But it is of great
importance, especially for every young person, to have in his heart a true, genuine,
and abiding love of God.

It is said that the decisive battles to be fought are with the devil, the world,
and the flesh. However, with the power of love - the love of God - all these can be
conquered. It is only when the ardent love of God dwells in one’s heart that he may
hope to speak of victories. The history of the world, the pages of sacred history, and
the history of each individual alike teach us that without love, there can be no
victory.

Love, in a general sense, conquers both good and evil things. Think of what
inspired heroes in all ages and led them to achieve immortal deeds of glory. What
inflamed the heart of Napoleon the Great, pushing himself forward without rest and

WHAT IS CADETSHIP?

There is more to the glamour and prestige that has always been associated
with the Philippine Military Academy; that is, the sacrifice and truth. Blood, sweat, and
tears are behind all of these.

First, it is blood, for it is the individual alone who can make himself survive the
continuously fluctuating changes and pressures of Academy life.

Second, is sweat - it is the painful process of changing from the carefree ways
of civilian life to the exacting demands of military life.

Third, are tears for the joy, pride, and feeling of fulfillment of having survived
obstacles, something between life and death.

Let it be known, however, that nothing can be a much better source of pride
than being able to conquer one’s weaknesses and turn them into strengths. Life
begins with a very young man so eager to join the ranks of the “long gray line,”
attracted by its glamour, only to be led down the wrong path upon entering and
leaving sooner than he came.

The “Beast Barracks” or Summer Training is something that this same young man
feels is too much for him. But it takes some attitude and courage, or guts, so to speak.
Once he is in, he is exposed to things he has never dared to think of before. He does
things he cannot imagine and wonders how they are done.

Anyway, it is every cadet’s goal as he prays to aspire above the level of
common life and to adhere to the patterns of their creed - truth, nobility, and
excellence.
The Summer Camp Training is a near-perfect program of development and
training. One has to survive and surmount it through thick and thin. The feeling to quit
is there after a rough time of one month or more.

But when Incorporation Day comes, every sacrifice is compensated. It is better
that one finds out for oneself what it really is like to be a part of this closely-knit big
family, that is, the Academy.

HANNIBAL, THE GREAT

Carthage, a great city-state in North Africa, had grown into power. She had
extensive colonies in the African continent, conquered Spain, and was in constant
warfare with the Roman Empire and its satellite cities. The war, which had been going
on between Rome and Carthage for nearly a century, had been indecisive, with the
Carthaginians having lost and won as many battles as the Romans.

In Carthage, there arose a general, Hannibal, who almost destroyed the
Roman Empire. No general had ever beaten the famed Roman army in as many
battles as Hannibal had, and no army had caused so much fear and destruction as
Hannibal’s army did.

Hannibal conceived of attacking the Romans in Italy. It was a feat never
before made or even dared by any army. He began his invasion with 90,000-foot
soldiers, 12,000 horsemen, and 40 elephants. He reached the foot of the Alps and
crossed these mountains in nine days. Then, he met the Roman armies.

By swift maneuvers, Hannibal managed to meet the Roman armies one by one.
The sight of the giant elephants charging them brought terror to the Roman cavalry.
They fled from the fight and were easily defeated. On one occasion, Hannibal found
himself completely surrounded. He ordered his army to fasten burning torches on the
cattle horns. At midnight, he drove the animals toward a heavily defended enemy
front. The terrible sight frightened the Roman ranks and destroyed them completely.

In many of these battles, Hannibal’s forces were often outnumbered, but his
elephants' juggernaut, the swiftness of his movements, and his brilliant command

gave him victory. For 16 years, Hannibal roamed the Italian peninsula, defeating all
the armies sent against him.

Meanwhile, powerful Roman forces had been sent to Carthage. Hannibal was
then recalled defending Carthage. However, his forces had been decimated in the
Italian campaign.

At Zama, near Carthage, the powerful Roman army met Hannibal’s forces. Here,
Hannibal met his defeat with a loss of 20,000 men. When peace was concluded, the
Romans demanded Hannibal’s surrender to Rome.

To escape, Hannibal committed suicide.

opts: Neutralizing Carthaginian cavalry and luring elephants into lanes

opts: Defiance against Roman pursuit despite political recovery in Carthage
Loyalty to Carthage over personal survival
Fear of capture after Zama victory

A GOOD TURN DESERVES ANOTHER

In life, there are many things that happen which are least expected.
When these things turn to blessings, people’s hearts are softened, and they
look up above to praise Him in glorious words. Some may just leave
occurrences and daily happenings to fate and may keep everything to
themselves.

But have you ever gone out of your way to do something for
someone and had it go unnoticed? Very often it is difficult to believe that
doing good to others is worth the effort, especially when we don’t receive
a “thank you” in return. And yet, serving without looking for a reward is just
like walking with God peacefully. As Christians, we should not display a
cash-and-carry attitude, expecting immediate appreciation for the good
we do. We must remember that someday he will richly reward us.

A magazine article told of a businessman who facilitated his dealings
in the car business with a very young foreigner. The latter bought a new car,
and a very fast and honest transaction took place between them. Short of
some thousand pesos to complete the full payment, the businessman
agreed to collect the amount after two weeks. Two weeks passed, but the
buyer still could not produce the amount as his money had not come yet.
So a grace period was given and extended to another two weeks. Finally,
the deal was over. Everything was paid for.

Ten years later, the young man had become the sole purchasing
agent for the Saudi Arabian Contractor’s Association. To repay the
businessman’s hospitality and to show his gratitude for all the conveniences

afforded to him, he placed a million-dollar order for 500 heavy dump trucks
and 200 pickups. The businessman blinked his eyes with disbelief. “It’s
unbelievable!” he exclaimed. “I just can’t believe it, but it’s true.” The good
he had done was rewarded years later, beyond his wildest imagination.

As the lines rightfully say: "Be not weary in your serving; Do your best
for those in need. Kindness will be rewarded, By the Lord who prompts the
deed."

COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS

Directions: Choose the letter of the correct answer.

items.text: What is the primary theological lesson the text draws from the businessman's story?
opts: God rewards only those who expect immediate payment for good deeds.
Patience in serving others leads to unexpected, abundant blessings over time.
Business success depends on trusting strangers without any risk.
Gratitude from others is unnecessary if faith is strong enough.

items.text: How does the text contrast a "cash-and-carry attitude" with Christian service?
opts: It portrays the attitude as more efficient for daily life than selfless acts.
It equates it to expecting instant rewards, unlike serving God without anticipation.
It suggests both approaches yield the same long-term results.
It recommends it for non-Christians but not believers.

items.text: The story of the young foreigner illustrates which key idea about rewards?
opts: Good deeds must be repaid within two weeks to be meaningful.
Grace periods in transactions guarantee future loyalty.
Business deals with foreigners always lead to profit.
Small acts of kindness can yield massive returns after a decade.

items.text: According to the text, why might people doubt the value of unnoticed good deeds?
opts: Due to a lack of verbal thanks, making the effort seem wasted.
Because blessings always come quickly and visibly.
Since fate handles all outcomes without human input.
As serving God requires public displays for validation.

items.text: What does the closing poem reinforce about the overall message?
opts: Rewards come only from human gratitude, not divine prompting.
One should serve only those who can reciprocate immediately.
Persistent kindness, even when tiring, is divinely rewarded.
Weariness in serving proves a lack of true faith.

THE LION IS DYING

The lion is the largest and most celebrated member of the cat family.
It has an apparently large-sized head because of the great mane which
covers its head, neck, and shoulders. By the time the lion is five or six years
old, it can weigh more than 500 lbs and can be over 9 ½ feet long from the
tip of its nose to the tip of its tail.

The lion has the reputation of being fearless, but it is more accurate
to describe it as sly. Its instincts are like those of a house cat, and it hunts like
a cat. It quietly stalks its prey, then, making a short, quick bound, lands on it.
It mauls and bites the head of its victim until its neck is broken, and its veins
and arteries are torn open.

The lion will eat anything it can find. While in the prime of its strength,
it will hunt all sizes of deer, zebras, and even buffaloes. However, as it grows
older, it may live on rodents, scorpions, and tiny creatures, even rotting
meat.

The lion was at one time known as the king of the jungle. The jungles
of Africa, Asia Minor, and India were once the lion’s domain. But man has
been slowly but surely exterminating the species. The lion has disappeared
in Asia Minor, Iran, and even in many parts of Africa. The remnants of the
lion family in Asia are now confined to Northwestern India’s GIR forest, a
reservation. There, some 160 lions remain, a pathetic remnant of a once
prolific species.

However, even in its sanctuary, the lions are losing their natural prey
of deer and wild buffaloes because men have encroached on the
sanctuary and have domesticated the buffaloes. The lions are forced to

slaughter and feed on domesticated buffaloes, and the herdsmen
retaliate by killing the lions.

The king of the jungle is fast becoming extinct. Unless man gives the
lions a place where they can live and multiply peacefully, and where their
natural diet of deer and other animals can also live, many may never see a
lion again except in museums or in picture books.

It declines to scavenging rodents and rotting meat out of necessity
It avoids small creatures to preserve strength ​

opts: Humans expanded jungles there for protection
The species thrives despite losing Asian Minor and African ranges
Man's extermination reduced it to a "pathetic remnant" of 160 lions

opts: Lions gain more deer prey from domestication

When any misfortune or ill luck comes our way, we often ask, "Why me, God?
Why should this happen to me?" Then we examine ourselves as to whether we are
right in professing our faith or giving the appearance of being one who believes in
the professed faith. Something dictates that perhaps it would be better if we ask,
"What can I learn from this? What is God teaching me?"

This story is told by a missionary in China many, many years ago about a
woman who boarded a train with him in Europe. The first thing the missionary
noticed was her radiant face, so sweet, and troubles seemed far from existence.
They talked about anything under the sun, and her face would brighten up when
mission and religious work were discussed. Obviously, she had not experienced
trying circumstances.

As the train sped off and their talk turned into intimate conversation, the
missionary observed that the woman's right hand was missing, and in its place was
a steel hook. As their talk continued, the missionary learned that this lady friend had
been a missionary in India, had contracted a lung disease, and had been sent
home to die. So, she returned to her native country, Sweden, bought a farm, and
worked daily on it.

One day, while she was working on a threshing machine, her right hand was
cut. It was a big blow, a great misfortune in her life, but she accepted it as one of
life's trials. She continued: When my hand was cut off, I immediately looked up and
said, "Lord, what do you really want me to do now that my right hand is gone?
What work? I was not asking why but what?"

What a brave woman! She deserves all the praises this world possesses with
her unflinching courage. Her strength of character is really commendable. God
used her to turn her farm into a home for the aged, the sick, and the feeble. She is
still there, bringing blessings to the unfortunate.

How many adverse circumstances come into your life? Our nature is to
question God's designs and workings. He just wants you to show the genuineness of
your faith and the adequacy of His grace. So stop asking why. God will show you
what.

Jaime L. Cardinal Sin was born on August 31, 1928, in New Washington, Aklan, to
Juan Sin and Maxima Lachica. He was ordained as a priest on April 3, 1954; served as
the first Rector of St. Pius X Seminary in Roxas City from 1957 to 1967; appointed
Auxiliary Bishop of Jaro in March 1967 and later Archbishop of Manila on March 19,
1974. Finally, he was named a Cardinal at the Consistory on May 26, 1976. His chosen
motto was “Serviam,” which means “to be a servant.” Cardinal Sin generously gave
himself in complete service and absolute devotion to God and His flock. He displayed
dynamic and militant leadership, which was his inspiration in his deep faith and
commitment to lead his people to Jesus Christ.

During his elevation to the Cardinalate, he urged everyone to join him in a
revolution, a revolution of love. Heeding the needs of his people, he tirelessly fought
for the ideals of freedom, truth, and justice. He believed in the separation between
the Church and State. Nevertheless, he asserted that the relationship between the
two should be collaborative rather than adversarial.

Through his inspired leadership, he united the Filipino people to make the
democratic process work in our country, and thus emerged as “People Power.”
Cardinal Sin’s contagious sense of humor seemed to have become a byword. His wit
and wisdom presented to us the partnership between humor and intellectual insight.
He thought of himself as an elder brother in the task that the Lord had given him. Full
of hope for a more humane citizenry, he turned to everyone on this land to tell them,
“Let us choose the way of peace. And the way of peace is the way of justice and
truth, the way of deep respect before God for the rights of each one.”

This was one of his favorite lines: “Man achieves the fullness of his humanity
when his dignity is respected, when his freedom to do good is protected. Working
hand in hand, the Church and the State can do so much to prevent man’s
dehumanization.” Before his death in 2006, he had assailed the continuing graft and
corruption in the government and had called for a more vigorous and unrelenting
drive against these. His interest called for a change not only in the government but
the private sector as well.

People all over the world are thrilled when athletic meets

communities.

                                 THE SMALLEST FISH IN THE WORLD

         Before 1925, the "tabios" was thought to have been the smallest fish in the
world. A full-grown "tabios" measured a fraction over eleven millimeters. The
"tabios" is found in Lake Buhi, in the Bicol Region of Luzon.



         In 1925, Dr. Albert Herre, an ichthyologist, was assigned by the American
government to identify and describe Philippine fishes. From a collection of the
Philippine National Museum, he found the prototypes of a still smaller type of fish.
There were 75 of the tiny fish which he named Pandaka Pygmaea in a bottle. They
were so small that the "tabios" appeared big by comparison.



         When Dr. Herre went back to the
United States, he sent a few specimens
to   the     Stanford    National    Science
Museum.       Dr.   Herre’s   findings   were
doubted because this fish remained a
rarity. No one had ever seen a live
specimen of the fish that Dr. Herre
claimed was the smallest fish in the
world.



         On February 28, 1951, Ricardo Esguerra, one of the marine biologists
working in the saltwater experiments station of the Bureau of Fisheries in Malabon,
Rizal, excitedly called up the Bureau’s main office and announced that he had
found live specimens of the Pandaka. Inocencio Ronquillo, an expert of the
Bureau, hurried to the experiment station and studied the tiny fish which had
eluded scientists for many years. He measured and weighed them. To confirm his
findings, Ronquillo wrote to the curator of Stanford University Museum of Natural
Science and asked for some specimens of the fish that Dr. Herre had taken before.

Finally, Dr. Leonard Schulz, the museum’s representative, pronounced that they
were one and the same type. Thus after 25 years, the Philippines could at least
claim to have the world’s smallest fish. The Pandaka has now been found in
various parts of the Philippines.



    The smallest fish is known under the scientific name of Pandaka Pygmaea.
Samples have been sent to the museums and aquariums of cities all over the
world.

The Pandaka’s average length when full-grown is 9.66 millimeters or about the size
of a grain of rice. It has a moderately elongated body that is wedge-shaped
when viewed from above. Its head is large in proportion to its size. Its eyes protrude.
It has two rows of teeth on either side of the jaw, the outer teeth being larger and
more widely set than the inner row.




                                COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS


1. Why was the discovery of Pandaka pygmaea in the Philippines in 1925 considered
historically important?
         A. It showed that all tabios populations had gone extinct
         B. It was then regarded as the smallest known fish in the world
         C. It was the first marine fish ever described from the Philippines

         D. It proved that all small fish in the Philippines were juveniles




2. What was Dr. Albert Herre’s main role in the history of Pandaka pygmaea?
         A. He first described and named Pandaka pygmaea in 1925

         B.He reclassified tabios as Pandaka pygmaea in 1951

       C.He proved that Pandaka pygmaea lives only in deep ocean trenches

       D.He led a campaign to ban fishing of all small fish in the Philippines




3. How did Ricardo Esguerra contribute to the story of Pandaka pygmaea in 1951?
       A. He replaced Pandaka pygmaea with tabios in scientific classification
       B. He officially declared Pandaka pygmaea extinct in the wild
       C. He moved all remaining Pandaka pygmaea to foreign aquariums
       D. He rediscovered Pandaka pygmaea in the Philippines after fears it had
       disappeared


 4. In historical discussions, why is the local fish known as tabios often mentioned
       alongside Pandaka pygmaea?
       A.Tabios and Pandaka pygmaea are the same species under different general
       B.Tabios is the scientific name that replaced Pandaka pygmaea
       C.Tabios was initially thought to be the true smallest fish, later replaced by
       Pandaka pygmaea
       D.Tabios is a local small fish whose fame was overshadowed by Pandaka
       pygmaea as the "smallest fish"


 5. Which statement best describes the typical habitat historically associated with
       Pandaka pygmaea in the Philippines?
       A. Clear, fast- flowing mountain streams
       B. Shallow coastal or estuarine areas, often near mangroves
       C. Deep, open- ocean pelagic zones
       D. High- altitude crater lakes far from the sea


  6. From a biological perspective, why is the tiny adult size of Pandaka pygmaea
       scientifically intriguing?
       A. It demonstrates that only deep- sea fish can become very small
       B. It challenges ideas about the lower size limits of vertebrate bodies

      C. It proves that all small fish grow into large fish later
      D. It shows that small fish cannot reproduce successfully


 7. Historically, how did the "smallest fish in the world" label affect public and scientific
      attention toward Pandaka pygmaea?
      A. It shifted all attention away from Philippine biodiversity
      B. It led to the immediate banning of all fishing in its habitat
      C. It turned Pandaka pygmaea into a globally cited example of extreme
      miniaturization
      D. It caused scientists to ignore Pandaka pygmaea as unimportant



   8. What does the historical replacement of tabios in popular discussion by
       Pandaka pygmaea as the "smallest fish" mainly illustrate?
       A. That local fish names are always incorrect
       B.That only foreign scientists can discover important species
       C.That large fish are more important than small fish
       D.That scientific records and media can reshape which species the public
       notices


9. Why is it important for modern students in the Philippines to learn about the historical
discovery and rediscovery of Pandaka pygmaea?
      A. It teaches only that foreign scientists are superior
      B. It shows that biodiversity is only found in other countries
      C. It highlights the value of both foreign and Filipino contributions to
      understanding local biodiversity
      D. It proves that small fishes are useless for food

10. What conservation lesson can be drawn from the story of Pandaka pygmaea’s
      small size and specialized habitat?
      A.Conservation is only needed in remote, untouched wilderness areas
      B.Only large, commercially valuable fish deserve protection
      C.Protecting mangroves and coastal wetlands can help safeguard even the

                    THE OLYMPIC GAMES



      People all over the world are thrilled when athletic meets
are held in various parts of the globe. World sports bring together
athletes from all over. Do you know when and how these Olympic
games came about?



      The first Olympic games originated in Ancient Greece. These
games were first held during the Panhellenic celebrations. Every
four years, patriotic and religious games were held during the
celebrations. The year 776 B.C. marked the first of such a recorded
festival. The Greeks then began to keep their calendar by
"Olympiads" from this date or by the four-year span between the
games.



      Simplicity marked the first Olympic games. It was said that
the first consisted of only a foot race of about 200 yards on the
plain near the small City of Olympia. As years passed, the kinds of
games were increased and led to competitions that brought
forward national pride and unity. The competitions were based on
fair rules of sportsmanship and justice. However, at first, only Greek
citizens were allowed to take part in the games. The winners were
crowned with laurel and awarded wild olive and palm wreaths.
Winners were also given many special privileges in their respective
communities.



      During the reign of the Roman rulers, these games went
down to the level of carnivals and circuses. Theodosius, one of the
Roman emperors, prohibited the holding of the games in 394 B.C.
For almost 2,300 years, no Olympic games were held.

understanding would develop.



      In 1896, Baron Pierre de Coubertin was able to enlist nine
